nodes.summary: Both decision values are reachable from `s` (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson, 1985, §3). The impossibility proof keeps a run in bivalent states forever.
nodes.title: Bivalent state

nodes.summary: Let there be at least two processes, and let `a` satisfy agreement (no reachable state has decided two values) and CSLib's `PseudoTermination 1` (a decision reachable from every reachable state without any one process). If a reachable state $s$ is bivalent and the message $m$ is in flight in $s$, then some state $t$ reachable from $s$ without receiving $m$ still has $m$ in flight, and receiving $m$ in $t$ leads to…
nodes.title: A bivalent configuration survives any pending event

nodes.summary: Let each decision value be decided in some reachable state, and let a decision be reachable from every reachable state without the participation of any one process (CSLib's `PseudoTermination 1`). Then some input assignment has a bivalent initial state. This is Lemma 2 of Fischer, Lynch and Paterson (1985), in CSLib's model.
nodes.title: A bivalent initial state

nodes.summary: With at least two processes, no deterministic asynchronous message-passing algorithm solves consensus tolerating $f \ge 1$ crash faults. Solving consensus means, in CSLib's `Cslib.FLP.Algorithm.Consensus`: in every reachable state all decided values agree and each is the input of some process, and in every admissible run (fair, with at most $f$ faulty processes) every process that is not faulty decides.
nodes.title: FLP impossibility of asynchronous consensus (CSLib form)

nodes.summary: Let there be at least two processes and let `a` be partially correct: no reachable state has decided two different values, and each value $b$ is decided in some state reachable from some input. Then some admissible run with at most one faulty process never decides: no process decides at any time. This is Theorem 1 of Fischer, Lynch and Paterson ("no consensus protocol is totally correct in spite of one fault"),…
nodes.title: FLP impossibility of asynchronous consensus, original form

nodes.summary: If from a state $s$ the schedule $xs_1$ leads to $s_1$ and the schedule $xs_2$ leads to $s_2$, and every message received in $xs_1$ goes to a process of a set $ps$ while every message received in $xs_2$ goes to a process outside $ps$, then $xs_2$ can be applied to $s_1$ and $xs_1$ to $s_2$, and both lead to the same state. This is Lemma 1 of Fischer, Lynch and Paterson (1985), in CSLib's model: schedules run by…
nodes.title: Commutativity of disjoint schedules

nodes.summary: If there are at least two processes and every admissible run of `a` with at most one faulty process decides (some process decides at some time), then `a` satisfies `PseudoTermination 1`: from every reachable state a decision can be reached using only the processes of any set that misses at most one process.
nodes.title: Deciding runs give reachable decisions

nodes.summary: `ReachWithout a m s t` holds when $t$ is reachable from $s$ by a schedule that never receives the message $m$. In Lemma 3 of Fischer, Lynch and Paterson (1985) these states form the set $\mathcal{C}$ of configurations reachable from $C$ without applying the event $e = (p, m)$; since messages can be delayed arbitrarily, $m$ stays in flight in all of them.
nodes.title: Reachability without an event

nodes.summary: `Valent a s b` holds when some state reachable from `s` by the algorithm `a` has decided $b$. In the terms of Fischer, Lynch and Paterson (1985, §3), $b$ belongs to the set $V$ of decision values of the configurations reachable from $s$; $s$ is bivalent when $|V| = 2$ and $b$-valent when $V = \{b\}$.
nodes.title: Valence of a state

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
